overview.text: The Rhine (Rhein in German, Rhin in French, Rijn in Dutch) is a major western European river connecting the Swiss Alps to the North Sea. Its Alpine headstreams join in eastern Switzerland; the river then reaches Lake Constance and continues west to Basel, north along the Upper Rhine to Bingen, and through Germany toward the Netherlands. In the Dutch delta it branches into several waterways, including the Waal, Nederrijn and IJssel, before reaching the sea. The International Commission for the Hydrology of the Rhine Basin gives its official length as 1,232.7 kilometers. The Rhine matters beyond its route: its watershed links nine states, so water use, flood management and protection require international cooperation.

key_facts.text: The Vorderrhein and Hinterrhein meet at Reichenau, Switzerland, to form the Alpine Rhine.
The Alpine Rhine flows into Lake Constance; its lower course forms borders between Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Austria.
The Upper Rhine runs from Basel to Bingen, and Alpine snowmelt contributes to higher flow in early summer.
At Lobith, on the German–Dutch border, the Rhine divides into delta waterways, including the Waal, Nederrijn and IJssel.
The Rhine basin commission reports an official river length of 1,232.7 km; it notes that other length figures can depend on mapping scale and how the river’s path through lakes is measured.
Water from nine states flows via the Rhine into the North Sea, making international cooperation important for managing shared water and competing uses.
